'''Roy Dyckhoff''' (4 March 1948 – 23 August 2018) was a British [[mathematician]], [[logician]] and [[computer scientist]] who worked in [[logic]] and [[proof theory]] in the Department of Pure Mathematics and later Computer Science at the [[University of St Andrews]].<ref name="standblog0">{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/csblog/2018/11/13/dr-roy-dyckhoff-a-eulogy/|title=Dr Roy Dyckhoff: A Eulogy|website=St Andrews Computer Science Blog|date=13 November 2018 |access-date=1 June 2025}}</ref> He is known for his discovery in 1992 of a [[Decidability (logic)|terminating]] [[sequent calculus]] for [[Intuitionistic logic|intuitionistic]] [[Propositional calculus|propositional logic]].<ref name="contfree">{{Cite journal |last=Dyckhoff |first=Roy |title=Contraction-free sequent calculi for intuitionistic logic |journal=[[Journal of Symbolic Logic]] |volume=57 |issue=3 |year=1992 |pages= 795–807|doi=10.2307/2275431|s2cid=30194066 }}</ref><ref name="troel">{{cite book|author1=Anne Sjerp Troelstra|author-link=Anne Sjerp Troelstra|author2=Helmut Schwichtenberg|author2-link=Helmut Schwichtenberg|title=Basic proof theory|year=2000|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-77911-1|edition=2nd}}</ref> His [[Erdős number]] was 3.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rd.host.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/|title=Roy Dyckhoff's page at St Andrews|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150515054528/http://rd.host.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/|archive-date=2015-05-15|access-date=1 June 2025}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Roy Dyckhoff was born on 4 March 1948, in [[Manchester]], to Eric Bernard Charles Dyckhoff, a solicitor, and Muriel Edith Turner. He had an older sister.<ref>{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=Deaths, Dyckhoff |date=11 November 1998 |page=22 |issue=66356 |column=Personal Column}}: "DYCKHOFF - Eric Bernard Charles, Solicitor, of Cheadle, Cheshire. Died peacefully on November 8th. 1998 after a short illness. Widower of Muriel and Jean and loving father of Elisabeth and Roy. Father-in-law of Cecillia, and grandfather of Livia and Max."</ref> His mother died on 6 October 1955, when he was seven years old. Later remarrying in 1959,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=64B5dFTLyrvj9C7T52eR9w&scan=1|title=Marriage 1938 - Eric Dyckhoff & Turner|accessdate=3 June 2025|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}<br/>{{Cite web|url=https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=FQJQ%2F43M5VQgFYce2Xv53w&scan=1|title=Death 1955 - Muriel Dyckhoff|accessdate=3 June 2025|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}<br />{{Cite web|url=https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=XHlbt1QUAHR0cKnPkGyThg&scan=1|title=Marriage 1959 - Eric Dyckhoff & Wilson|accessdate=2 June 2025|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}</ref> his father ran the law firm Dyckhoff and Johnson in [[Cheadle, Greater Manchester|Cheadle]] and founded the Cheadle Civic Society.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cheadlecivicsociety.uk/about-us|title=About Us|website=Cheadle Civic Society|access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref>

Raised in [[Cheshire]], he spent his youth at boarding school [[Winchester College]].<ref name="standblog1">{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/csblog/2018/09/04/dr-roy-dyckhoff/|title=Dr Roy Dyckhoff|website=St Andrews Computer Science Blog|date=4 September 2018 |access-date=1 June 2025}}</ref> Dyckhoff grew an interest in church [[Bell-ringer|bell-ringing]], joining a group of ringers there.<ref name="sacrobit">{{Cite web|url=https://www.sacr.org/index.php/association/obituaries/48-obituary-roy-dyckhoff|title=Obituary Roy Dyckhoff|website=Scottish Association of Change Ringers|author=Peter Williamson|access-date=1 June 2025}}</ref> Dyckhoff spent a year programming punch-cards at [[English Electric Leo Marconi]].<ref name="standblog0"/> Enrolling in an undergraduate program at [[King's College, Cambridge]] in 1966, he studied [[mathematics]] but also spent a year attending only lectures in [[Middle Eastern studies]].<ref name="kingsannual">{{Cite web|url=https://www.kings.cam.ac.uk/sites/default/files/documents//kings-annual-report-2019-web.pdf|title=Annual Report 2019|website=King’s College, Cambridge|access-date=1 June 2025}}</ref> During his time at King's College, he rang a [[peal]] at [[Trumpington]] with a band of first year students.<ref name="sacrobit"/>

After receiving his undergraduate degree, he pursued further studies at [[New College, Oxford]], completing a [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] in Mathematics in 1974. His dissertation, ''Topics in General Topology: Bicategories, Projective Covers, Perfect Mappings and Resolutions of Sheaves'', was supervised by Peter J. Collins and [[Dana Scott]].<ref name="mathgen" /> He was later appointed Fellow of [[Magdalen College, Oxford]].<ref name="kingsannual"/>

== Career ==
In 1975, Dyckhoff became a lecturer in the Department of Pure Mathematics at [[University of St Andrews|St Andrews]], later moving to Computer Science in 1981<ref name="standblog1"/> due to the reduced funding under the [[Margaret Thatcher|Thatcher government]].<ref name="kingsannual"/> Early in his scientific career, he contributed to [[topology]] and [[category theory]].<ref name="mathgen" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dyckhoff |first1=Roy|last2=Tholen|first2=Walter|title=Exponentiable morphisms, partial products and pullback complements|journal=[[Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra]] |volume=49|issue=1-2|year=1987 |pages= 103–116 |doi=10.1016/0022-4049(87)90124-1}}</ref> Applying his experience in programming and interest in formal logic, he shifted to [[theoretical computer science]] and [[Mathematical logic|logic]] where he came to specialise in [[proof theory]] and [[automated theorem proving]].<ref name="kingsannual" />

His investigations into [[intuitionistic logic]] led him to discover the contraction-free [[intuitionistic]] [[sequent calculus]] G4ip in 1992.<ref name="contfree"/><ref name="tableux">{{Cite conference |last1=Graham-Lengrand|first1=Stephane|last2=Negri|first2=Sara|author2-link=Sara Negri|title=Remembering Roy Dyckhoff|book-title=Automated Reasoning with Analytic Tableaux and Related Methods|conference=28th International Conference, TABLEAUX 2019|location=London, UK|year=2019 |pages=xiv--xvii|url=https://www.mv.helsinki.fi/home/negri/roy_mem_tableaux.pdf|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-29026-9}}</ref> The contraction rule was known to be problematic for [[Automated theorem proving|backward proof-searches]] as it can cause unwanted loops. By producing a contraction-free calculus and proving the admissibility of contraction, Dyckhoff provided the first [[Decidability (logic)|terminating]] [[Intuitionistic logic|intuitionistic]] [[Propositional calculus|propositional]] [[sequent calculus]]. Such a calculus was anticipated in 1950s by the founder of the [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] school of [[game theory]], [[Nikolai Nikolayevich Vorobyov (mathematician)|Nikolai Vorobyov]]. Dyckhoff's calculus laid the groundwork for subsequent terminating proof systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Iemhoff |first1=Rosalie|author1-link=Rosalie Iemhoff |title=The G4i Analogue of a G3i Sequent Calculus|journal=[[Studia Logica]] |volume=110 |year=2022 |pages= 1493–1506|doi=10.1007/s11225-022-10008-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Additionally he settled a question posed by [[Georg Kreisel]] in 1971 on the relationship between cut-elimination, substitution and normalisation. He co-authored several papers with [[Sara Negri]] on topics involving [[intermediate logics|intermediate]] and [[modal logic]]s.<ref name="kingsannual"/>

His later works investigated [[Aristotelian logic|Aristotelian]] and [[Stoic logic]]. With [[Susanne Bobzien]] he proved the decidability of Stoic logics in a Hertz-[[Gerhard Gentzen|Gentzen]] system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dyckhoff |first1=Roy|last2=Bobzien|first2=Susanne|author2-link=Susanne Bobzien |title=Analyticity, Balance and Non-admissibility of Cut in Stoic Logic |journal=[[Studia Logica]] |volume=107 |year=2019 |pages= 375–397|doi=10.1007/s11225-018-9797-5 |hdl=10023/13269 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Dyckhoff married Cecilia Meredith in 1970,<ref name="kingsannual"/> and the couple spent their time between St Andrews and Glengarry, [[Invergarry]] in the [[Scottish Highlands]]. They had two children: a daughter, Livia, and a son.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rd.host.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/|title=Roy Dyckhoff's page at the Department of Computer Science at St Andrews|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080518174837/http://www-theory.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~rd/|archive-date=2008-05-18|access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/2007/09/halo-ai/|title=Smart Tweaks Amp Up Halo 3's Killer AI|website=Wired|author=Clive Thompson|author-link=Clive Thompson (journalist)|date=27 September 2007}}</ref> As a Tower captain at the [[St Salvator's Chapel]], Dyckhoff rang for various services, occasionally involving his wife and children in the ringing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sacr.co.uk/images/documents/annual%20reports/2014%20SACR%20Annual%20Report%20Website.pdf|title=2014 Annual Report|website=Scottish Association of Change Ringers|access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref> He was involved in the installation of additional bells in 2003 and later in 2010 to commemorate the consecration of the chapel and the founding of the university.<ref name="sacrobit"/> He was also an avid hiker and bell-ringer in his free time, and supported the [[Mountain Bothies Association]].<ref name="standblog1"/>

Dyckhoff died on 23 August 2018 from an [[acute myeloid leukemia]].<ref name="kingsannual"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aslonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Jan2019newsletter-1.pdf|title=ASL Newsletter - January 2019|website=Association for Symbolic Logic|access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref>
